youtube.title: Kuril Islands Dispute: Why Russia and Japan Still Have No Peace Treaty
youtube.description:
The Kuril Islands dispute is why Russia and Japan have still not signed a peace treaty, eighty years after the Second World War. Russia has held four islands off northern Japan since 1945, while Japan calls them its Northern Territories and says they are its own. We explain the Russia Japan border dispute on the map, from the 1855 Treaty of Shimoda to the 1956 Joint Declaration, and what each side wants.

On the map we trace every line drawn across this water, from the 1855 Treaty of Shimoda to Yalta, San Francisco and the 1956 Joint Declaration. We set out each side's case in its strongest form and the three outcomes analysts describe, and what each would change on the map.

{CHAPTERS}

youtube.title_before: Kuril Islands Dispute: 4 Islands Keeping Russia and Japan From Peace

sources.claim: The nearest islet lies 3.7 km from Cape Nosappu, Hokkaido
sources.source: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Japan, 'Northern Territories' pamphlet and website (current edition)

sources.claim: Russia has held all four islands since 1945
sources.source: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Japan, 'Japan's Northern Territories' (occupation 28 Aug to 5 Sep 1945); Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Kuril Islands'

sources.claim: Russia and Japan never signed a WWII peace treaty; 81 years since 1945
sources.source: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Japan, 'Japan-Russia Relations' (2024); Russian MFA statement, 21 March 2022

sources.claim: The Kuril chain runs about 1,200 km with about 56 islands
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Kuril Islands'

sources.claim: Japan calls them the Northern Territories; Russia the Southern Kurils, part of Sakhalin Oblast
sources.source: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Japan; Charter of Sakhalin Oblast (Russian Federation)

sources.claim: Areas: Iturup 3,167 km², Kunashir 1,489 km², Shikotan 253 km², Habomai 95 km²; total about 5,000 km²
sources.source: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Japan, 'Northern Territories' data

sources.claim: Kunashir lies about 16 km from Hokkaido's Notsuke peninsula
sources.source: Hokkaido Government, Northern Territories Affairs Office

sources.claim: About 20,000 people live on the islands
sources.source: Russian official estimates as reported by Reuters (2022) and Rosstat 2021 census district figures

sources.claim: Yuzhno-Kurilsk on Kunashir is the seat of the Yuzhno-Kurilsky district, under Sakhalin Oblast
sources.source: Sakhalin Oblast administration

sources.claim: Cold Oyashio and warm Kuroshio currents meet off the islands, making rich fishing grounds
sources.source: Japan Meteorological Agency, ocean current data; Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Kuril Islands'

sources.claim: Analysts describe the Sea of Okhotsk as a protected bastion for Russia's Pacific Fleet missile submarines
sources.source: IISS, 'The Military Balance' (2023); CSIS analyses of Russia's Pacific Fleet

sources.claim: In 2016 Russia announced Bal and Bastion coastal missile systems on Kunashir and Iturup
sources.source: Russian Ministry of Defence, Pacific Fleet newspaper 'Boyevaya Vakhta', Nov 2016; Reuters, 22 Nov 2016

sources.claim: Vice Admiral Yevfimy Putyatin led the Russian mission to Japan in 1855
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Yevfimy Vasilyevich Putyatin'; Lensen, 'The Russian Push Toward Japan' (Princeton, 1959)

sources.claim: Treaty of Shimoda, 7 February 1855, signed by Putyatin and the shogunate's envoys Kawaji Toshiakira and Tsutsui Masanori, set the border between Iturup and Urup; Sakhalin left undivided
sources.source: Treaty of Commerce, Navigation and Delimitation (Shimoda), 1855; MOFA Japan translation; Lensen, 'The Russian Push Toward Japan' (1959)

sources.claim: 1875 Treaty of Saint Petersburg: Japan gave up Sakhalin claims for all Kuril Islands to Shumshu
sources.source: Treaty of Saint Petersburg, 7 May 1875; MOFA Japan

sources.claim: 1905 Treaty of Portsmouth gave Japan southern Sakhalin
sources.source: Treaty of Portsmouth, 5 September 1905

sources.claim: Yalta, February 1945: 'The Kuril islands shall be handed over to the Soviet Union'
sources.source: Yalta Agreement on the Entry of the Soviet Union into the War Against Japan, 11 February 1945 (US Department of State, FRUS)

sources.claim: Japan says it is not bound by Yalta, to which it was not a party
sources.source: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Japan, 'Japan's Northern Territories' Q&A

sources.claim: USSR declared war on Japan on 8 August 1945
sources.source: Soviet declaration of war, 8 August 1945; Encyclopaedia Britannica

sources.claim: Hiroshima was bombed on 6 August 1945, two days before the Soviet declaration of war
sources.source: US Strategic Bombing Survey, 'The Effects of Atomic Bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki' (1946); City of Hiroshima, official records

sources.claim: The Soviet offensive into Manchuria began on 9 August 1945 and into southern Sakhalin on 11 August 1945
sources.source: David M. Glantz, 'August Storm: The Soviet Strategic Offensive in Manchuria' (2003); Hasegawa, 'Racing the Enemy' (Harvard, 2005)

sources.claim: 1941 Soviet-Japanese Neutrality Pact, in force from 25 April 1941 for five years, i.e. until April 1946; Japan says it was broken
sources.source: Soviet-Japanese Neutrality Pact, 13 April 1941, Article 3; MOFA Japan

sources.claim: USSR gave notice in April 1945 it would not renew the pact
sources.source: Molotov statement to Ambassador Sato, 5 April 1945 (Hasegawa, 'Racing the Enemy', 2005)

sources.claim: Soviet landings on Shumshu began 18 August 1945, three days after the emperor's surrender broadcast
sources.source: Hasegawa, 'Racing the Enemy' (Harvard, 2005)

sources.claim: Iturup taken 28 August; Kunashir and Shikotan by 1 September; Habomai 3-5 September 1945, after the 2 September surrender
sources.source: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Japan, 'Japan's Northern Territories'

sources.claim: 17,291 Japanese lived on the four islands; all were sent to Japan by 1949
sources.source: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Japan; Cabinet Office, Northern Territories Affairs

sources.claim: Soviet decree of 2 February 1946 incorporated southern Sakhalin and the Kurils into the RSFSR
sources.source: Decree of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet of the USSR, 2 February 1946

sources.claim: San Francisco Peace Treaty signed 8 September 1951 by Japan and 48 Allied nations; Article 2(c) renounces the Kurile Islands; USSR attended but did not sign
sources.source: Treaty of Peace with Japan, 8 September 1951 (UN Treaty Series vol. 136)

sources.claim: Japan's position: Iturup and Kunashir are not among the renounced Kuriles; Habomai and Shikotan belong to Hokkaido
sources.source: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Japan; PM Yoshida's speech at San Francisco, 7 September 1951

sources.claim: 1956 Joint Declaration, signed 19 October 1956 by Prime Minister Ichiro Hatoyama and Soviet Premier Nikolai Bulganin, ended the state of war; Article 9 transfer of Habomai and Shikotan after a peace treaty
sources.source: Joint Declaration by the USSR and Japan, 19 October 1956 (UN Treaty Series vol. 263)

sources.claim: Both parliaments ratified the 1956 Joint Declaration; it entered into force on 12 December 1956
sources.source: Joint Declaration by the USSR and Japan, UN Treaty Series vol. 263 (entry into force 12 December 1956 on exchange of instruments of ratification); MOFA Japan

sources.claim: Habomai and Shikotan are 348 km², about 7 percent of the area claimed
sources.source: Calculated from MOFA Japan area figures

sources.claim: Japan admitted to the United Nations on 18 December 1956
sources.source: United Nations, member states list

sources.claim: Dulles in August 1956 linked a Japanese concession to Okinawa, by historians' accounts
sources.source: Kimie Hara, 'Japanese-Soviet/Russian Relations since 1945' (Routledge, 1998); Hasegawa, 'The Northern Territories Dispute' (1998)

sources.claim: Japan renewed its security treaty with the United States in January 1960
sources.source: Treaty of Mutual Cooperation and Security between Japan and the United States of America, signed Washington, 19 January 1960 (MOFA Japan)

sources.claim: Soviet note of 27 January 1960 made transfer conditional on withdrawal of foreign troops from Japan
sources.source: Soviet aide-memoire to Japan, 27 January 1960 (MOFA Japan)

sources.claim: 1993 Tokyo Declaration by Yeltsin and Hosokawa named all four islands
sources.source: Tokyo Declaration on Japan-Russia Relations, 13 October 1993

sources.claim: 2001 Irkutsk Statement by Putin and Mori confirmed the 1956 Declaration as the basic legal document
sources.source: Irkutsk Statement, 25 March 2001

sources.claim: Medvedev visited Kunashir on 1 November 2010, the first Russian leader to do so
sources.source: Reuters, 1 November 2010; Kremlin.ru

sources.claim: Shinzo Abe met Putin 27 times
sources.source: Nikkei Asia and The Japan Times, August-September 2020

sources.claim: Singapore, 14 November 2018: agreement to accelerate talks on the basis of the 1956 Declaration
sources.source: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Japan, summit summary, 14 November 2018

sources.claim: Japanese newspapers read Singapore as a shift toward two islands first; the government said its position was unchanged
sources.source: Asahi Shimbun and Nikkei, 15 November 2018; Chief Cabinet Secretary press conference, 15 November 2018

sources.claim: Russia's foreign ministry cites Yalta, the 1951 renunciation and Article 107 of the UN Charter
sources.source: Russian MFA statements, e.g. spokeswoman Zakharova, 2019; UN Charter Article 107

sources.claim: Putin in December 2018 questioned whether US forces could be based on islands Japan received
sources.source: Kremlin.ru, Vladimir Putin's annual news conference, 20 December 2018

sources.claim: 2020 constitutional amendment forbids actions aimed at alienating Russian territory
sources.source: Constitution of the Russian Federation, Article 67(2.1), in force 4 July 2020

sources.claim: Grave visits from 1964; visa-free exchanges from 1992
sources.source: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Japan, 'Exchanges with Russian residents of the Northern Territories'

sources.claim: Surviving former islanders number a few thousand, average age near 90
sources.source: League of Residents of Chishima and Habomai Islands, as reported by Kyodo News (2025)

sources.claim: On 21 March 2022 Russia suspended peace treaty talks and visa-free visits after Japan's sanctions
sources.source: Russian MFA statement, 21 March 2022; Reuters, 21 March 2022

sources.claim: Mitsui (12.5%) and Mitsubishi (10%) kept stakes in Sakhalin-2
sources.source: Mitsui & Co. and Mitsubishi Corp. press releases, August-September 2022; annual reports FY2023

sources.claim: Sakhalin-2 LNG loads at Prigorodnoye on Aniva Bay, southern Sakhalin; tankers reach Japan through La Pérouse Strait, west of the islands
sources.source: Sakhalin Energy, Prigorodnoye production complex and shipping information; Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'La Pérouse Strait'

sources.claim: Russia supplied about 9 percent of Japan's LNG in 2021
sources.source: Japan Ministry of Finance trade statistics, 2021

sources.claim: Russia stationed fighter jets at Iturup in 2018; Japan protested, as it did over the 2016 coastal missiles
sources.source: Russian Ministry of Defence, August 2018; MOFA Japan protest, 2018; Chief Cabinet Secretary Suga press conference, 22 November 2016 (protest over missile deployment)

sources.claim: Japanese boats fish near the islands under a 1998 agreement; Russia suspended it in June 2022 over payments
sources.source: Japan-Russia agreement on fishing operations, 1998; Kyodo News, 7 June 2022

sources.claim: Abe and Putin agreed on joint economic activities on the four islands in December 2016 at Nagato
sources.source: MOFA Japan, Japan-Russia summit press statement, 16 December 2016

sources.claim: Five pilot project areas listed in 2017; pilot tourist trips ran in October 2019
sources.source: MOFA Japan, 7 September 2017; The Japan Times, 31 October 2019
